9
Which statement defines force?
A
When a force acts on a body that is free to move, the force is the product of the mass of the
body and its acceleration.
B
When a force acts on a body that is free to move, the force is the rate of change of
momentum of the body.
C
When a force acts on a body that is free to move, the force is the work done by the force
divided by the distance moved by the body.
D
When a force acts on a lever and causes a moment, the force is the moment divided by the
perpendicular distance of the force from the pivot.

hints: Notice the word defines - all four statements can give a correct value in some situation, but only one is true generally for any mass and any force.
Recall the general form of Newton's second law linking resultant force to momentum $p = mv$: $F = \Delta p / \Delta t$.
Check the other statements for limits: product $ma$ needs constant mass, $W/s$ needs constant force along the displacement, and $moment/d$ only applies to turning about a pivot.
walkthrough: Identify what is asked: the statement that defines force for any body free to move, not a formula that works only in a restricted case.
State the governing physics: Newton's second law defines resultant force as the rate of change of momentum, $F = \Delta p / \Delta t$, where $p = mv$.
Note that if mass $m$ is constant, this becomes $F = m\Delta v / \Delta t = ma$, so the product of mass and acceleration is a consequence, not the definition.
Check the work and moment statements: $F = W/s$ follows from $W = Fs$ and $F = moment/d$ follows from $moment = Fd$, so they calculate force from its effects in those contexts.
Therefore only the rate of change of momentum statement is the general definition. This is option B.

A.explanation: This gives $F = ma$, which is true only when mass is constant and so is a special case, not the general definition.

B.explanation: Force is defined by Newton's second law as the rate of change of momentum, $F = \Delta p / \Delta t$.

C.explanation: This rearranges $W = Fs$ to $F = W/s$, which applies only for a constant force in the direction of motion, not the definition of force.

D.explanation: This rearranges $moment = Fd$ to $F = moment/d$, which describes the force needed for a particular turning effect, not what force is.
